main_claims: TUPA is the first parser for UCCA, a cross-linguistically applicable semantic representation framework.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents TUPA, the first parser for UCCA, a semantic representation framework characterized by reentrancy, discontinuous structures, and non-terminal nodes. The core argument is that TUPA, particularly its BiLSTM-enhanced variant, effectively addresses these unique structural challenges and significantly outperforms existing parsing techniques adapted for UCCA. The paper logically progresses from defining the problem and UCCA's properties, through the detailed design of TUPA's novel transition set and features, to a comprehensive experimental evaluation. The reasoning is generally strong, with clear linkages between the identified challenges, the proposed solution, and the empirical results. However, some methodological choices, such as greedy inference for TUPA against beam-search-enabled baselines, and the inherent limitations of conversion procedures for baselines, introduce minor points of concern regarding the absolute fairness of comparison, though the paper attempts to mitigate these by reporting upper bounds.

P2: The lack of a UCCA parser limits its applicability.
C1: TUPA is the first parser for UCCA, addressing this gap (C1).

M1: TUPA employs a novel transition set and features, including BiLSTMs, specifically designed to handle UCCA's general DAG structures (C3, C8, C11).
M2: An experimental setup is designed, including in-domain and out-of-domain UCCA corpora, a yield-based evaluation metric for primary and remote edges (A5, A7).
M3: Baselines are established by converting UCCA graphs to bilexical graphs and trees, acknowledging conversion-induced limitations and reporting upper bounds (A2, C9).
R1: TUPABiLSTM achieves substantially superior F-scores on both primary and remote edges, in-domain and out-of-domain, compared to TUPAMLP and all baselines (C6, C7).
R2: Baselines, especially tree parsers, perform poorly on remote edges due to their inherent structural limitations and the conversion process (C9).
C2: The novel transition set and BiLSTM features are effective for UCCA parsing (C8).
C3: TUPA's general DAG parsing capability has broader implications for other semantic DAG structures and languages with discontinuous structures (C4, C11).
C4: A UCCA parser will enable new tasks and support deeper semantic structure integration in applications (C13).

strengths.title: Coherent Design of Novel Transition Set
strengths.description: The proposed transition set is logically designed to specifically address UCCA's complex properties, including NODE for non-terminals, LEFT/RIGHT-REMOTE for reentrancy, and SWAP for discontinuities. This demonstrates a strong fit between the problem and the algorithmic solution.
evidence: Building on previous work on parsing reentrancies, discontinuities and non-terminal nodes, we define an extended set of transitions and features that supports the conjunction of these properties.
For every X ∈ L, NODEX creates a new node on the buffer as a parent of the first element on the stack, with an Xlabeled edge.
LEFT-REMOTEX and RIGHT-REMOTEX do not have this restriction, and the created edge is additionally marked as remote.
To handle discontinuous nodes, SWAP pops the second node on the stack and adds it to the top of the buffer...

Although TUPA still outperforms these baselines, the absence of beam search in TUPA might underestimate its full potential or introduce a slight imbalance in the comparison, as beam search can significantly improve performance in transition-based parsing.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces TUPA, the first parser for Universal Conceptual Cognitive Annotation (UCCA), a semantic representation framework characterized by reentrancy, discontinuous structures, and non-terminal nodes. The authors propose a transition-based parsing approach with a novel transition set and features, including a BiLSTM feature extractor. The methodology involves training TUPA on the UCCA Wikipedia corpus and evaluating its performance against various baselines (bilexical dependency graph parsers and tree parsers) that are adapted via conversion procedures to approximate UCCA structures. Evaluation is conducted using a yield-based Labeled Precision, Recall, and F-score for primary and remote edges, in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings. The core argument is that TUPA, particularly with the BiLSTM feature extractor (TUPABiLSTM), achieves superior performance, demonstrating the effectiveness of its design in handling UCCA's complex graph properties. My audit confirms the methodological soundness of the proposed system and its evaluation, while highlighting areas where the comparative analysis and metric justification could be further strengthened for absolute validity.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript introduces TUPA, the first parser specifically designed for Universal Conceptual Cognitive Annotation (UCCA), a semantic representation framework. The core argument is that UCCA presents a unique parsing challenge due to its combination of reentrancy (DAG structures), discontinuous units, and non-terminal nodes, a conjunction of properties not fully supported by any single existing parser. To address this, TUPA proposes a novel transition set and leverages bidirectional LSTMs for feature extraction. The paper evaluates TUPA against various strong baselines, including bilexical dependency graph parsers and tree parsers, by converting UCCA graphs to approximate structures for baseline compatibility. The experimental results demonstrate TUPA's, particularly TUPABiLSTM's, superior performance in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings, especially in handling remote edges crucial for reentrancy. The authors position TUPA as a significant step towards enabling wider adoption of UCCA and informing the development of parsers for other complex semantic DAG structures.

Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Codes: I1, I12

Content: eview earlier and ask more experienced people in your network for feedback. Some ACs may also offer feedback for reviews that come in good time. Irresponsible reviewers and chairs. Unfortunately, with the growing number of conference submissions, there have been more and more cases where reviewers or chairs sign up for service and then simply disappear without a warning, are late without a warning, or submit (meta-)reviews that are completely unacceptable in their quality (e.g. extremely terse, unprofessional in tone, LLM-generated). Starting in October 2024, ARR provided the authors with the opportunity to report common issues with reviews (e.g. rude reviews, ‘not novel’ criticism without providing references, etc.) The ACs will see such reports, if any, judge their merit, and take them into account when writing the meta-review. A similar functionality has now been developed for meta-reviews, with author issue reports viewable for senior area chairs. Since the reviewer and AC guidelines may also seen by the authors during the response period, some sections of these guidelines now have codes for (meta-)review issues (I1-I12) that can be reported by the authors. More details here and here. Starting in May 2025, ARR also adopts the new policy on the ‘highly irresponsible’ (meta-)reviewers. The program chairs and ARR EiCs will consider the egregious cases reported by chairs (on their own judgement or based on author reports), including the cases of extremely terse reviews, unprofessional tone, and LLM-generated reviews.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
